muc.title: A rainy night, dark clothes
muc.text: On a rainy night, a person in dark clothes steps into the road. The camera is only half sure it's a person, radar sees something moving slowly, and LiDAR sees a shape 1.7 meters tall.

muc.title: Three clues that match
muc.text: Combining several sensors into one conclusion is called sensor fusion. The human shape, the walking speed and the blurry figure on camera all match, so the AI is sure enough to brake.

muc.title: Each eye reports a number
muc.text: For distance, each eye reports its own number, and each has its own error. The camera's error is the largest.

muc.title: Trust some eyes more
muc.text: The AI doesn't take a simple average. It trusts the eyes with smaller errors more. Worked out, LiDAR gets 58 percent of the weight, radar 37 and the camera 4, giving 23.8 meters.

muc.title: Combined is more accurate
muc.text: The channel ran 10,000 trials with a true distance of 24 meters. LiDAR was off by 64 cm on average, while the combined estimate was off by only 49, better than even the best single eye.

muc.title: When the eyes disagree
muc.text: Fusion makes mistakes too. When the eyes report opposite things or the AI misreads them, the car can brake hard on an empty road, known as phantom braking. In 2022 the US opened an investigation after hundreds of complaints like this.

muc.title: The blue dot on your map
muc.text: The blue dot in Google Maps is also sensor fusion, of GPS, compass and motion sensors. If the beam around the dot spreads wide, tap the dot, choose compass calibration and move your phone in a figure eight.
